# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles the population histories of 3886 towns,
fortresses and frontier outposts across the 38 historical regions of
Eastern Europe and Siberia from 1400AD to the Treaty of Nystad in
1721AD. Spanning Hanseatic ports on the Baltic, Magdeburg-law market
towns in Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine, Muscovite stone citadels,
timber forts along the Oka, Belgorod and Simbirsk defence lines, Ural
salt and ironworks towns and Siberian river *ostrogi*, the tables trace
how war and frontier settlement reshaped urban life over three
centuries. While mid-seventeenth-century wars and early
eighteenth-century plague cut back the older towns of Lithuania,
Belarus, Right-Bank Ukraine and the Baltic coast, new garrison and
trading towns grew rapidly across Left-Bank and Sloboda Ukraine, the
southern Russian black earth, the Middle Volga, the Urals and Siberia,
culminating in the rise of Saint Petersburg after 1703AD.

# Methodology

This gazetteer traces the population history of 3886 towns, fortresses
and frontier outposts across the 38 historical regions of Eastern Europe
and Siberia between 1400AD and 1721AD: 1.965 in Russia and Siberia
(Regions 18-38), 1.184 in Ukraine and Crimea (Regions 9-17), 287 in
Belarus (Regions 5-8) and 258 across the Baltic provinces, Lithuania and
Old Finland (Regions 1-4)
[\[1\]](#ref-Vodarsky1973)[\[2\]](#ref-Vodarsky1977)[\[3\]](#ref-Kabuzan1963)[\[4\]](#ref-Palli1996)[\[5\]](#ref-Dunsdorfs1962)[\[6\]](#ref-Kiaupa2000)[\[7\]](#ref-KarpachevKozlovsky1972)[\[8\]](#ref-Yakovenko2006)[\[9\]](#ref-Dolgikh1960).
These settlements span Hanseatic ports on the Baltic, Magdeburg-law
market towns (*miasteczka*) in Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine, Swedish
border castles in Karelia, Cossack regimental capitals, timber and stone
strongholds along the Oka, Belgorod and Simbirsk defence lines, Ural
salt and ironworks towns and Siberian river *ostrogi*
[\[10\]](#ref-Tikhomirov1962)[\[11\]](#ref-Bernotas2013)[\[12\]](#ref-Sharukho2010)[\[13\]](#ref-Rezun1989)[\[14\]](#ref-Zhigalov2024).

Town populations across the benchmark dates are drawn from Baltic
ploughland audits (*Hakenrevisionen*) and burgher rolls, the 1528AD
Lithuanian muster (*Popis*) and hearth-tax (*podymne*) registers,
Muscovite land books (*pistsovye knigi*), the 1646AD and 1678AD
household censuses (*perepisnye knigi*), Peter the Great’s First Soul
Revision (1719-1721AD, *revizskie skazki*), Left-Bank Ukrainian census
books (1666AD) and Cossack regimental rolls, Ottoman tax registers
(*tahrir defterleri*) for Crimea and Kefe and Siberian fur-tribute
(*yasak*) and inspection (*dozornye*) books
[\[15\]](#ref-Shapiro1974)[\[16\]](#ref-Morzy1965)[\[17\]](#ref-Vasiliauskas2012)[\[18\]](#ref-Saloheimo1976)[\[19\]](#ref-Irtenina2022)[\[20\]](#ref-Ozturk2019)[\[21\]](#ref-Pokrovsky1984).
Dates before a town was founded or after it was abandoned are marked
with a hyphen (-).
